lessonTitle: Mechanical and Adhesive Joints: Bolts, Rivets and Bonds in Thin Sheet

blocks.text: A 0.8 mm aluminium panel on a kitchen extractor is bolted at its corners, and within a month hairline cracks run from the bolt holes. The same panel bonded to its frame with a structural adhesive shows no cracks and carries the load happily, until someone prises a corner with a screwdriver and the whole bond peels away in seconds. Same joint, two loadings, opposite outcomes.

blocks.markdown: Joints that can be taken apart (screws, bolts) and permanent joints (rivets, adhesives) behave very differently in thin sheet. A hole removes material and concentrates stress, while a bonded joint spreads load over an area. Choosing a joint means matching the load path, the materials, and whether it has to be disassembled.

Poor: bearing and tear-out at holes

blocks.caption: Representative comparison for thin sheet.

blocks.markdown: The strength of the common mechanical joints is found from the area that carries the load. Rivets and bolts in single shear fail by shearing the shank or by crushing (bearing) the sheet at the hole; the weaker of the two governs. An adhesive lap joint is carried by shear stress over the overlap.

blocks.caption: Capacity of n fasteners of diameter d in single shear (shear strength tau_s) and bearing (bearing strength sigma_b on sheet of thickness t), and of an adhesive lap joint of width b and overlap length L with shear strength tau_a. The joint fails at the smallest value.

blocks.title: Adhesive lap joint capacity
blocks.prompt: Two aluminium strips 25 mm wide are bonded with an overlap of 12.5 mm. The adhesive has a shear strength of 20 MPa (typical). Find the failure load and the allowable load with a safety factor of 3.

steps.text: Bond area is the width times the overlap length.
Failure load: shear strength times area (MPa x mm^2 gives N).
Allowable load: divide by the safety factor of 3.

blocks.answer: Failure load 6.25 kN; allowable load about 2.08 kN.

blocks.title: Riveted joint: shear or bearing?
blocks.prompt: Three aluminium rivets of diameter 4 mm (shear strength 150 MPa) join sheet 1.5 mm thick whose bearing strength is 300 MPa (typical values). Find the joint capacity and the governing failure mode.

steps.text: Area of one rivet in shear: $\pi d^2/4$ = 12.57 mm^2.
Bearing capacity: 3 x 4 x 1.5 x 300 = 5400 N.
The joint fails at the smaller load, so bearing governs.

blocks.answer: Capacity 5.4 kN, governed by bearing in the sheet. Using a thicker sheet or more rivets raises it.

blocks.markdown: **Shear versus peel.** In a lap joint pulled along its length, the adhesive is stressed in **shear** across the whole overlap, and a structural adhesive may carry 15 to 30 MPa. If the joint is loaded so that one adherend is lifted away from the other, the load is concentrated on a line at the edge of the bond and the adhesive is stressed in **peel** (or cleavage). The same adhesive may carry only a few newtons per millimetre of width in peel, which is orders of magnitude less than in shear.

blocks.title: Load adhesives in shear, avoid peel
blocks.text: Adhesives are strong in shear and compression because the whole bond area works together, and weak in peel and cleavage because the load is concentrated on a thin line at the bond edge. Design joints so that loads are shear along the bond, add overlap for strength, and use straps, scarf joints or mechanical fasteners to remove peel loads.

items: Use a generous overlap so load is carried over a large area.
Prefer double-lap or strap joints to reduce the bending that causes peel at the overlap ends.
Add a few rivets or screws at the edges to stop peel from starting.
Prepare the surfaces (clean, degrease, abrade) and follow the cure schedule.
Avoid designs that put the bond in tension across the thickness at one edge.

blocks.markdown: **Selecting a method.** Ask four questions: what materials are being joined (can they be welded or do they react galvanically?), how is it loaded (shear, tension, peel, vibration?), must it be dismantled for service, and what are the volume and cost? Thin sheet that must be dismantled uses screws or bolts with washers; permanent light sheet assemblies use rivets or adhesive; dissimilar materials or smooth, hole-free surfaces favour adhesive.

rows: Large area, thin sheet, no holes

blocks.title: Adhesive joints depend on preparation
blocks.text: Contaminated or smooth surfaces, wrong cure temperature or time, and long-term moisture exposure can reduce the strength far below the datasheet value. A joint that cannot be inspected should be designed with generous safety factors.

points: For thin sheet, adhesives spread load over an area without holes, rivets give fast permanent joints, and bolts allow disassembly but concentrate stress at the hole.
Mechanical joint capacity is the smaller of the shear and bearing capacities; an adhesive lap joint carries load in shear over the overlap area.
Adhesives are strong in shear and weak in peel, so design for shear and use overlap, straps or added fasteners to avoid peel; choose the method from the materials, loading and disassembly needs.

questions.stem: Which is the main advantage of an adhesive joint over a bolted joint for 0.8 mm aluminium sheet?

options.text: It spreads the load over the bonded area and needs no holes in the thin sheet
It can be disassembled easily for repair
It is unaffected by surface contamination
It carries high loads in peel

questions.correctOptionText: It spreads the load over the bonded area and needs no holes in the thin sheet

distractorRationale.b: Adhesive joints cannot be dismantled without damage.
distractorRationale.c: Adhesives are sensitive to contamination and surface preparation.
distractorRationale.d: Adhesives are weak in peel; their strength is in shear.

questions.explanation: A bonded joint distributes the load over the whole overlap, avoiding the stress concentrations and bearing failure at holes in thin sheet. Its limits are peel loads, preparation and permanence.

questions.stem: Why does an adhesive lap joint fail at a much lower load when one strip is lifted away from the other (peel) than when the strips are pulled along their length?

options.text: Peel concentrates the load on a thin line at the edge of the bond instead of sharing it over the whole area
The adhesive is chemically different in the two cases
The overlap area is smaller in peel
The strips are weaker in tension than in shear

questions.correctOptionText: Peel concentrates the load on a thin line at the edge of the bond instead of sharing it over the whole area

distractorRationale.b: The adhesive is the same; the stress distribution differs.
distractorRationale.c: The geometric overlap is the same.
distractorRationale.d: The strength of the adherends is not the issue; the bond line fails.

questions.explanation: In shear the whole overlap area carries the load together, but in peel the load is applied at the end of the bond, so one narrow strip carries it and the adhesive fails progressively along the line. That is why a peel strength is quoted per unit width.

questions.stem: Which design change most effectively reduces peel stresses at the ends of an adhesive lap joint?

options.text: Using a double-strap joint, or adding a rivet at the end of the overlap
Reducing the overlap length
Using a thicker layer of adhesive
Loading the joint across the thickness at one edge

questions.correctOptionText: Using a double-strap joint, or adding a rivet at the end of the overlap

distractorRationale.b: A shorter overlap reduces the capacity and does not remove peel.
distractorRationale.c: A thick adhesive layer generally weakens the joint and does not stop peel.
distractorRationale.d: This loads the joint in peel or cleavage.

questions.explanation: A double-strap joint balances the load path and reduces the bending that opens the ends of the bond, while an end rivet clamps the edge against peel. Other changes either weaken the joint or increase peel loading.

questions.stem: A carbon-fibre panel must be joined permanently to an aluminium frame without heat. Which method is most suitable?

options.text: Adhesive bonding
Fusion welding
Brazing at 600 degrees C
Soldering at 250 degrees C

distractorRationale.b: The two materials cannot be fusion welded together.
distractorRationale.c: Brazing temperatures would damage the composite.
distractorRationale.d: Soldering would not bond the composite and the heat is damaging.

questions.explanation: An adhesive joins dissimilar materials without heat and spreads the load, avoiding drilling that cuts the fibres. The thermal methods would damage the composite or cannot wet it.

questions.stem: An access panel on a machine must be removed monthly for service. Which joint should be chosen?

options.text: Screws or bolts with washers
Structural adhesive
Blind rivets
Brazing

distractorRationale.b: The adhesive joint cannot be removed without damage.
distractorRationale.c: Blind rivets must be drilled out to remove the panel.

questions.explanation: The need for repeated disassembly points to threaded fasteners, which are the reversible option. Rivets, adhesives and brazed joints are permanent and would need destroying to open.

questions.stem: A single-lap adhesive joint between two strips 20 mm wide has an overlap of 15 mm. The adhesive's shear strength is 18 MPa. What is the allowable load in N with a safety factor of 2?
questions.explanation: The bond area is $20\times15=300$ mm^2, so the failure load is $18\times300=5400$ N. Dividing by the safety factor 2 gives an allowable load of 2700 N.

questions.stem: Four rivets of diameter 3.2 mm (shear strength 140 MPa) join a sheet 1.0 mm thick with bearing strength 280 MPa. Each rivet is in single shear. Find the load capacity of the joint in N.
questions.explanation: Shear capacity is $4\times140\times\pi\times3.2^2/4=4504$ N, and bearing capacity is $4\times3.2\times1.0\times280=3584$ N. The joint fails at the smaller value, so bearing governs at 3584 N.

questions.stem: A peel test on a 25 mm wide bonded strip fails at a force of 40 N. A lap joint with the same adhesive and an overlap of 12 mm has shear strength 15 MPa. Compare the load per millimetre of width the joint carries in shear with the peel load per millimetre of width: what is the ratio shear : peel?
questions.explanation: The peel load per unit width is $40/25=1.6$ N/mm. In shear the load per unit width is $15\times12=180$ N/mm, so the ratio is $180/1.6=112.5$. The result shows why adhesive joints are loaded in shear.

questions.stem: Compare bolted, riveted and adhesive joints for a thin sheet metal enclosure, covering stress at the joint, disassembly and the effect on the sheet.
markingGuide: Bolted: removable but loads concentrated at holes, bearing and tear-out in thin sheet; loosening under vibration
Riveted: permanent, fast, holes needed, load by shear and bearing at few points
Adhesive: no holes, load spread over area, permanent, sensitive to peel and surface preparation
States which suits the enclosure with a reason such as access needs or sheet thickness
Notes that mechanical fasteners may be combined with adhesive
questions.explanation: The three joints differ in load transfer, reversibility and effect on the sheet. A good answer compares them against the enclosure's requirements before choosing one.

questions.stem: Explain why adhesive joints are best loaded in shear and should avoid peel, and describe two design measures that avoid peel in a bonded sheet joint.
markingGuide: Shear loading shares the load over the whole bond area
Peel concentrates the load along a narrow line at the bond edge
Adhesive peel strength is much lower than its shear strength per unit width
Measure: double lap or strap joint, or scarf joint
Measure: increase overlap, add an end rivet or screw, or redesign so loads act in shear
questions.explanation: The strength of a bonded joint depends on the stress distribution, which is uniform in shear and concentrated in peel. Design measures that balance or clamp the bond ends remove or reduce the peel component.
